title: Refs and the DOM
summary: A ref lets a React component keep a value without asking React to redraw the page when that value changes.
introduction: A ref lets a React component keep a value without asking React to redraw the page when that value changes. Use a ref to reach a text input and put the typing cursor in it. Compare this with state, which is used for values shown on the page.
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between a ref and state
Attach a ref to a DOM element and call its methods
Store timer ids and other mutable values in refs
Pass a ref to a custom component using the React 19 ref prop

blocks.text: `useRef(initialValue)` returns an object with one property, `current`, that React keeps the same between renders. You can read and write `current` freely, and doing so **never** causes a re-render. That is the whole API, and both of its uses follow from it: holding a DOM node, and holding any value that must survive renders but does not affect what is rendered.

Pass the ref object to the `ref` attribute of a JSX element. After React commits the element to the DOM, `ref.current` points at that node; before that, and after the element is removed, it is `null`.

blocks.text: Focus management, scrolling (`element.scrollIntoView()`), measuring (`element.getBoundingClientRect()`) and media control (`video.play()`) are the common cases. Do everything through the node's own DOM API, and do not change attributes or children that React renders, or the two will fight over them.

blocks.text: The ref counted correctly, but the screen only caught up when something else caused a render. That is the rule: if a value is used in the JSX, it is state; if it is only used inside handlers and effects, a ref will do.

blocks.text: The interval id is not displayed, so it does not belong in state, and a plain variable would be lost on the next render. The guard in `start` prevents two intervals running at once, and the effect's cleanup clears whatever interval is still running when the component unmounts.
Passing refs to your own components

A ref on a custom component does nothing by itself: `<TextField ref={r} />` has no DOM node to attach to. In React 19, `ref` arrives as an **ordinary prop**, so the component can forward it to the element it wants to expose. Before React 19 this required wrapping the component in `forwardRef`; that code still runs, but new code does not need it.

blocks.text: If you want to expose a small custom API instead of the raw node, `useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ focus() { ... } }))` does that. It is rarely needed; forwarding the node is usually enough.

Instead of a ref object you can pass a function. React calls it with the node when the element mounts, and in React 19 the function may return a cleanup that runs when the element unmounts. This is the tidiest way to set something up per element, such as an observer, without an effect.

blocks.title: Common mistake: reading a ref during the first render
blocks.text: `const el = ref.current; el.focus();` in the component body runs before the element exists, so `current` is `null` and the call throws. Refs are populated after commit. Use them in event handlers and effects, and never put `ref.current` in the JSX expecting the screen to follow it.

questions.question: In React 19, how does a function component receive a ref passed as `<Input ref={r} />`?
questions.explanation: React 19 passes `ref` like any other prop, so `function Input({ ref, ...props })` can forward it. `forwardRef` still works but is no longer necessary.

questions.question: Writing to `ref.current` causes the component to re-render.
questions.explanation: Refs are deliberately invisible to rendering. Only state and props (and context) trigger renders.

seo.title: React useRef – DOM Access and Mutable Values
seo.description: Learn useRef in React 19: focus and measure DOM elements, keep timer ids without re-rendering, pass ref as a prop to your own components and use ref callbacks.
